children: By Joe Flint and Ben Fritz
Disney is planning a restructuring of its television operation that's expected to result in hundreds of layoffs and the consolidation of divisions, according to people familiar with the matter.

Senior executives are currently working out details of the plan, which might not be finalized before the end of the year. It's the latest in a series of reorganizations since Josh D'Amaro became chief executive in March. The former parks chairman has sought to streamline a sprawling operation full of fiefdoms.
Layoffs have already hit marketing, Pixar, ABC News and ESPN. On Tuesday, Disney laid off more than 300 people, most of whom work in human resources and information technology.

Cuts are also in the works at Disney's legal and global affairs unit, which has about 1,000 employees. In a memo to staff, Disney chief legal and global affairs officer Horacio Gutierrez said his team "will be a much smaller organization than it is today," citing advances in automation. Deadline previously reported on the memo.
Most Hollywood studios have cut costs in recent years as they adjust to a world in which streaming profits are a fraction of what they earned from cable.
D'Amaro has responded by pushing Disney to think of itself as a unified digital entertainment operation.

Last month, he elevated former YouTube executive Adam Smith to chairman of streaming and named Silicon Valley veteran Karandeep Anand as Disney's chief technology officer. The entertainment giant hasn't previously had technology executives in such senior roles.

In August, Disney launched a voluntary early-retirement initiative targeting executives over age 50 with at least 10 years of experience. The company waited to see how many took the offer before moving forward with its TV plans, some of the people familiar with the matter said.

A primary goal for the TV reorganization is to structure the business in a way that makes sense for streaming customers, rather than around brands created decades ago for linear television, one of the knowledgeable people said.

Disney President and Chief Creative Officer Dana Walden, speaking at a Bloomberg conference Thursday, said the company is taking a bunch of divisions that have been run separately and "centralizing as a television business, not a bunch of silos."
She said "there is a need to constantly evaluate how you're structured" and "how big is the organization."

Disney Entertainment Television chairman Debra OConnell, who reports to Walden, is spearheading the plan. Her operation includes an array of production studios and brands, some of which Disney inherited in its 2019 acquisition of most of the entertainment assets of 21st Century Fox.

They include ABC Entertainment, 20th Television, Hulu Originals, Disney Kids & Family, National Geographic Content and Freeform. Each has its own executives that develop and produce programming-primarily for Disney+, Hulu, and the company's linear channels, as well as other outlets.
The reorganization is expected to affect some of the executives who run those units, the people familiar with the matter said.
ABC News is also under OConnell and further reductions are expected there as well, people close to that business said.

The long-running parade of layoffs at Disney began under D'Amaro's predecessor Bob Iger, during his second stint as CEO. The company employed 231,000 people as of the end of its fiscal 2025, most of whom work in its theme parks.
